## DATA 352/551: Modeling and Simulation

**Fall 2026**

**Instructor:** Prof. Yi Lu  
**Email:** [ylu1@drew.edu](mailto:ylu1@drew.edu)  
**Office:** HS 314  
**Lectures:** Wednesday, 6:00-8:30 p.m., HS 308 (in person)  
**Office hours:** R 12-2 (in-person HS314 or via [Google Meet](https://meet.google.com/osa-nsvf-dpk){target="_blank"}); or [by appointment](https://calendar.app.google/bSYSzjv5v5ybxvLt7){target="_blank"}


## Course Description

Covers techniques for modeling and simulating random systems that are otherwise complicated to study. Topics may include sampling from probability distributions, approximate sampling, Monte Carlo and MCMC methods, bootstrap, and simulation-based inference.

**Prerequisite:** CSCI 149, CSCI 150, STAT 120, or DATA 505.

## Learning Outcomes

Upon completing this course, students will:

- have a basic understanding of how simulation can be used in various applications;
- have a basic understanding of probability and statistical concepts;
- be able to use common parametric distributions to model random observations;
- be able to perform statistical inference using a few simulation-based techniques;
- be able to simulate random samples and random processes; and
- be able to design and implement simple algorithms to perform simulations.

## Text and Reading Materials

Topics in this class are relevant to a few different fields in statistics, especially probability and computational statistics.

- Reading materials will be posted on the course webpage throughout the semester.
- For probability, we will mostly use [*Introduction to Probability*](course_documents/Intro%20to%20Probability.pdf) (Grinstead and Snell, 2012), which is available online.
- For computational statistics, topics will roughly follow *Statistical Computing with R* (Rizzo, 2019). This book is not required for this class. It is more in-depth than the scope of this class and requires substantial statistical knowledge.

## Course Webpage

Course content will be posted on the [course webpage](https://lu08.github.io/teaching/DATA352/). Grades will be posted on Moodle. Check both the course webpage and Moodle frequently, and check your email regularly for important announcements.

## Programming

Lecture examples, sample code, and homework solutions will be given in R. It is acceptable to choose a different programming language. Some basics of R will be covered at the beginning of the semester. For simplicity, I will use RStudio; other popular IDEs for R include VS Code, Positron, and Jupyter Notebooks. Feel free to use any of these instead of RStudio.

## Late Work and Missed Assignments

**There are no make-ups in this class, even for excused absences.** Instead, your two lowest quiz grades and two lowest assignment grades are dropped. If you have to miss an exam, communicate with me as soon as possible. **All quizzes and exams must be taken in person; absolutely no exceptions.**

## Grading

Final grades are assigned according to the standard scale: A = 92 to 100; A- = 90 to 92; B+ = 88 to 90; B = 82 to 88; B- = 80 to 82; C+ = 78 to 80; C = 72 to 78; C- = 70 to 72; F = 0 to 70. If registered as an undergraduate: D+ = 68 to 70; D = 62 to 68; D- = 60 to 62; F = 0 to 60.

- **Homework quizzes (20%; two drops allowed):** Homework problems and solutions will be assigned roughly weekly. Homework is not collected; instead, a quiz will be given at the beginning of the lecture when the homework is due. Quiz content is directly based on the homework questions. There are no make-ups for this grade under any circumstance; the two lowest grades may be dropped.
- **In-class assignments (20%; two drops allowed):** These assignments occur during most lectures and are not announced ahead of time. Regular attendance and active participation in group assignments and class discussions are expected. There are no make-ups for this grade under any circumstance; the two lowest grades may be dropped.
- **Exams (3 $\times$ 20%):** There are three in-class exams: two midterms and one final. Exams are closed book, notes, and electronics. For each exam, you may use one double-sided 8.5-by-11-inch (or A4) reference sheet.

## Cross-Listed Class

Some exam components might differ for students registered in DATA 352 versus DATA 551. In general, the DATA 551 version will be slightly longer, more open-ended, and more comprehensive.

## Final Exam Policy

If extenuating circumstances occur, students may submit a Final Exam Reschedule request for review by the Associate Provost. Students may not negotiate a make-up date directly with the course instructor. Students may request to reschedule an exam only under the following circumstances:

- Two final exams scheduled at the same time;
- three final exams scheduled in one calendar day, in which case one exam will be rescheduled at the convenience of the instructor and the student; or
- serious illness or personal emergency, with documentation required for validation.

The final exam schedule is visible on the [Registrar's website](https://drew.edu/academic/office-of-the-registrar/registration/final-exam-schedule/) by the beginning of each semester. Students are expected to schedule travel plans **after** their final exams. Our final exam is scheduled for **Wednesday, December 16, 7:30-10:30 p.m.**

## Artificial Intelligence

I encourage you to explore artificial intelligence (AI) resources for learning purposes. When using AI, you must:

1. fully document and cite all material, including any code, graph, formula, table, mathematical equation, or other AI-generated material, in submitted work;
2. check information generated by AI and take full responsibility for its accuracy; and
3. be able to identify where and how you used any AI tools and how they contributed to your work.

If you have any doubts about what is acceptable, please discuss them with the professor.
